sentences.text: Savannasaurus was a medium-sized titanosaur measuring about 15 meters in length and weighing around 20 tons.
This animal stood approximately 3 meters at the shoulder.
A theropod tooth found near the holotype suggests a predator may have fed on the specimen.
This sauropod was found in the Late Cretaceous Winton Formation of Queensland, Australia, where David Elliot and his family first discovered it in March 2005.
Stephen Poropat and colleagues named the only known species, Savannasaurus elliottorum, in 2016.
The fossils come from the upper Winton Formation, a rock unit dated to about 93.9 million years ago at the Cenomanian-Turonian boundary.
Savannasaurus was likely a wide-gauge sauropod, standing and walking with its feet far apart from its midline.
The robust humerus is considered a likely adaptation to this wide-gauge stance.
Savannasaurus is classified as a basal member of Titanosauria that diverged early, rather than belonging to the specialized group Lithostrotia.
Mannion and colleagues found Savannasaurus within Saltasauridae in 2019 only when using equal weighting of characteristics, not implied weighting.
The sternal plates lacked the long ridges present on the bottom surfaces of most Neosauropoda.
These proportions made Savannasaurus extremely wide-hipped, a trait surpassed only by Opisthocoelicaudia and saltasaurines like Neuquensaurus.
Savannasaurus lived during the Cenomanian to Lower Turonian stages of the Late Cretaceous.
Palaeobiogeographic analysis suggests the ancestors of Savannasaurus were likely Asian.
It is debated whether the specific vertebral traits of Savannasaurus, such as the absence of hyposphene-hypantrum articulations, were unique adaptations or shared features with Diamantinasaurus.
Poropat and colleagues suggested that climate preferences might explain why Australian dinosaurs like Savannasaurus show affinities with Laurasian species.
